identity.title: The Value of Prediction in Identifying the Worst-Off

problem.claim: The paper examines how prediction affects welfare when policy prioritizes identifying and assisting the most vulnerable, including how prediction compares with expanding bureaucratic capacity.

contributions.claim: Develops mathematical models for understanding the relative effectiveness of prediction in surfacing the worst-off.
Includes a real-world case study of long-term unemployment among German residents.
Reports analytical frameworks and practical, data-driven tools intended to support principled policy design.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish prediction as one policy lever whose welfare impacts should be assessed relative to alternatives such as bureaucratic-capacity expansion.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report combining mathematical models with a real-world German unemployment case study to develop their assessment of prediction.
The authors report producing analytical frameworks and practical data-driven tools for policymakers designing these systems.

narrative_sequence.summary: Government programs increasingly use machine learning to prioritize assistance for people at greatest risk rather than optimize aggregate outcomes.
The paper examines the welfare effects of prediction in equity-driven settings and compares prediction with expanding bureaucratic capacity.
It uses mathematical models and a case study concerning long-term unemployment among German residents.
The authors present analytical frameworks and data-driven tools for principled policy-system design.

source_observation.claim: The abstract frames prediction as part of a broader policy comparison, explicitly placing it alongside bureaucratic-capacity expansion.

lessons.interpretation: This framing can make a technical intervention more decision-relevant by exposing trade-offs against an implementable alternative.
lessons.application: When presenting a predictive targeting method, define at least one competing policy lever and compare welfare implications under the same equity objective.
lessons.exception: This comparison may be unsuitable when alternatives cannot be represented consistently or when the study lacks information about their costs and effects.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative findings, directional comparison, or conditions under which prediction outperforms or underperforms capacity expansion.
Details of the mathematical models, case-study design, data, and practical tools are not provided.
